name: Disturbances of Respiratory Function
aliases: Disorders of lung ventilation and gas exchange

clinicalPearls: The respiratory system can be conceptualized as three functionally independent components: the lung (with its airways), the neuromuscular system (the force generated by respiratory muscles), and the chest wall (everything else, including the muscle mass itself, an obese abdomen, and an enlarged heart).

Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the passive resting volume where outward recoil of the chest wall is exactly balanced by inward recoil of the lung; at FRC, negative intrapleural pressure offsets positive intrapulmonary pressure giving an airway pressure of 0.

The combined respiratory system pressure-volume relationship is sigmoid: stiffness at high lung volumes is imparted by the lung, stiffness at low volumes by the chest wall (or airway closure), with compliance greatest in the mid-range where normal tidal breathing occurs.

Expiratory airflow limitation is a normal lung property arising from collapsible (not rigid) bronchial airways: as gas accelerates toward the mouth the Bernoulli effect lowers intraluminal and transmural pressure, narrowing the airway, so harder effort yields no net increase in flow.

Inspiratory airflow limitation is rarely caused by diffuse intrathoracic airway disease because more negative pleural pressure during inspiration increases airway transmural pressure and expands airways; instead, inspiratory flow limitation points toward extrathoracic/upper-airway narrowing (e.g., tracheal lesion, post-tracheostomy stricture).

Adequacy of alveolar ventilation is reflected in PaCO2: alveolar and arterial CO2 tensions are equal, the controller normally targets ~40 mmHg, so PaCO2 below 40 indicates hyperventilation and above 40 indicates hypoventilation, with ventilatory failure being extreme hypoventilation.

Only the tidal volume that exceeds the anatomic dead space delivers fresh gas to alveoli; dead space is increased functionally when ventilated lung receives no perfusion (e.g., distal to a large pulmonary embolus), 'wasting' that ventilation.
Oxygen uptake in normal lung is perfusion-limited rather than diffusion-limited: hemoglobin is typically fully saturated by the time blood traverses only about one-third of the alveolar capillary.

Hypoxemia from true shunt (perfusion of nonventilated lung) is refractory to supplemental oxygen, whereas hypoxemia from ventilation/perfusion heterogeneity (low V/Q regions) typically improves with oxygen therapy - a key bedside discriminator.

DLCO interpretation: it falls in diseases that thicken or destroy alveolar membrane (pulmonary fibrosis, emphysema), curtail the pulmonary vasculature (pulmonary hypertension), or reduce capillary hemoglobin (anemia); it can be elevated in asthma, polycythemia, and pulmonary hemorrhage.

In severe airflow obstruction, slowed expiratory flow prevents complete exhalation, raising operating FRC (dynamic hyperinflation / auto-PEEP); at these high volumes the system is less compliant, so the patient senses difficulty INHALING even though the root problem is EXPIRATORY obstruction.

A normal FEV1/FVC ratio does not exclude airflow obstruction: obstruction can raise residual volume and lower FVC, rendering the ratio 'artifactually normal' - lung volumes should scale together (~85-115% predicted) in health, so disproportion is a clue.
harrison.pathophysiology: Effective respiration requires tidal ventilation to freshen alveolar gas, perfusion of each alveolus proportional to its ventilation, and adequate diffusion of O2 and CO2 across the thin alveolar membrane (roughly 70 m2 of surface in about 7 L of thorax via multigenerational airway and vascular branching). Ventilation depends on the volume-related (elastic/static) and flow-related (dynamic) mechanical properties of lung, neuromuscular system, and chest wall; lung recoil rises with inflation while the passive chest wall stiffens at low volume. Disease deranges these properties in a limited number of ways: increased lung elastic recoil restricts volumes (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis lowers TLC/FRC/RV/FVC and DLCO but raises flow relative to volume); chest-wall abnormality (e.g., moderate obesity) blunts outward chest recoil and lowers FRC; reduced muscle strength (e.g., myasthenia gravis) lowers TLC and raises RV, reducing FVC/FEV1 as bystanders; decreased airway diameter (e.g., acute asthma) raises resistance and scoops the flow-volume loop; and decreased elastic recoil (e.g., severe emphysema) causes hyperinflation with very elevated TLC/FRC/RV and reduced DLCO. Gas-exchange failure (hypoxemia) results from low inspired oxygen tension, severe alveolar hypoventilation, perfusion of low-V/Q or unventilated (shunt) units, and, rarely, diffusion limitation; shunt blood disproportionately lowers arterial PaO2 because of the nonlinear oxyhemoglobin relationship. Hypercarbia accompanies disorders of ventilation, including severe obstruction and progressive restriction.
additionalDifferentials: Restrictive pattern from increased lung elastic recoil (e.g., idiopathic/interstitial pulmonary fibrosis)
Restrictive pattern from chest-wall abnormality (e.g., obesity, kyphoscoliosis)
Restrictive pattern from respiratory muscle weakness (e.g., myasthenia gravis, diaphragmatic paralysis, neuromuscular disease)
Obstructive pattern from airway narrowing (e.g., asthma, chronic bronchitis)
Obstructive pattern from loss of elastic recoil (e.g., emphysema)
Pulmonary vascular disease (suggested by isolated low DLCO with otherwise preserved volumes)
Upper/central airway obstruction (e.g., tracheal adenoma, post-tracheostomy stricture, tracheomalacia)
infectionMimics: Pneumonia or other alveolar-filling processes reduce respiratory system compliance and increase work of breathing, mimicking other causes of restrictive dyspnea
nonInfectiousMimics: Anemia (lowers DLCO and oxygen content, mimicking a gas-transfer defect)
Polycythemia or pulmonary hemorrhage (can elevate DLCO)
Obstructive sleep apnea with associated pulmonary arterial hypertension lowering DLCO in an obese patient
Cardiac causes of dyspnea (enlarged heart functioning as part of the chest-wall load)
additionalInvestigations: Spirometry (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, flow-volume loop) to characterize obstructive vs restrictive physiology and localize airway obstruction
Absolute lung volumes by inert-gas (helium/neon) dilution or body plethysmography (plethysmography preferred in airflow obstruction, as dilution underestimates trapped gas)
Single-breath diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO)
Arterial blood gas with calculation of the alveolar-arterial oxygen tension difference (A-a)DO2 and the alveolar gas equation
Pulse oximetry for noninvasive hemoglobin saturation; capnography (end-tidal CO2) for noninvasive ventilation assessment
Maximal inspiratory/expiratory mouth pressures and supine-vs-upright FVC to detect respiratory muscle / diaphragmatic weakness
Chest imaging: ultrasound, plain radiograph (PA and lateral), CT (with contrast and/or PET when indicated)
Further studies as guided by suspicion: bronchoscopy with lavage/biopsy, hypercoagulable and serologic testing, sputum analysis, echocardiography, surgical lung biopsy
redFlags: Hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen, suggesting true shunt physiology rather than simple V/Q mismatch
Rising PaCO2 above 40 mmHg indicating alveolar hypoventilation, with extreme elevation signaling impending ventilatory failure
Inspiratory flow plateau on the flow-volume loop, indicating extrathoracic/upper-airway obstruction
Precipitous fall in PaO2 on exertion in emphysema, reflecting inability to raise cardiac output across a destroyed pulmonary vascular bed
Supine FVC decrement greater than about 10-25% (versus the normal 3-8%) indicating significant diaphragmatic/neuromuscular weakness
Isolated reduction in DLCO with preserved spirometry and volumes, prompting evaluation for pulmonary vascular disease
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis is determined by the underlying disorder rather than the physiologic pattern itself; the same abnormalities may arise from very different diseases, so pulmonary function testing alone often cannot discriminate among conditions. Many functional disturbances are reversible (e.g., bronchodilator-responsive airflow obstruction in acute asthma), whereas others reflect fixed structural loss (e.g., capillary and alveolar destruction in emphysema or fibrosis) that progressively impairs gas exchange and exercise capacity.
pitfalls: Interpreting a normal FEV1/FVC ratio as excluding obstruction when raised RV has lowered FVC and made the ratio artifactually normal
Relying on single-breath inert-gas dilution in airflow obstruction, which underestimates true lung volumes because poorly ventilated regions do not receive the inert gas
Assuming alveolar hypoventilation alone explains severe hypoxemia at sea level breathing air - the alveolar gas equation shows this is uncommon unless barometric pressure is reduced (altitude)
Forgetting that a normal chest radiograph does not exclude respiratory disease, especially airway and pulmonary vascular disorders
Attributing a low DLCO to parenchymal disease without considering anemia, while overlooking that DLCO may be elevated in polycythemia or pulmonary hemorrhage
Misreading dyspnea on inhalation in severe obstruction as a primary inspiratory problem when it stems from dynamic hyperinflation due to expiratory flow limitation
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal severity grade applies; physiologic severity is judged by the degree of deviation from predicted values. Most lung-function measures are normal at 85-115% of predicted, and in health volumes scale together. Examples of marked derangement cited include severe emphysema (TLC ~130%, RV ~310%, FEV1 ~35% predicted, low DLCO ~40%) versus pulmonary fibrosis (TLC/FVC/FRC/RV ~60%, low DLCO). Airway resistance (Raw) is normally <2 cmH2O/L/s, and maximal mouth pressures >±60 cmH2O at FRC make significant muscle weakness unlikely.
